# voice-cascade

Python prototype of the **STT → LM → TTS** cascade voice agent, with a **swappable
LM stage** (Hugging Face Inference Providers *or* local MLX). Companion to the
PersonaPlex full-duplex evaluation — see
`~/Develop/realtime-persona/docs/personaplex-local-inference.md`.

```
 mic ─▶ Voxtral STT ─▶ text ─▶  LM (HF router | local mlx-lm)  ─▶ text ─clauses▶ Voxtral TTS ─▶ speaker
        (voxmlx)                 cascade/lm.py                      cascade/tts.py
```

## Why a cascade

PersonaPlex (full-duplex S2S) has ~160 ms first-audio and native barge-in but a
structurally **halting** speaking cadence. A cascade gives **smooth, controllable
speech** (the TTS plans whole utterances) and lets you use **any LM**, at the cost
of additive latency and turn-based (engineered) barge-in.

## The swappable LM stage

`cascade/lm.py` exposes one streaming interface with two backends, selected by
`LMConfig.engine` — mirroring Tsubaki's `provider.engine` switch:

```python
from cascade.lm import LMConfig, build_messages, make_lm

# Hugging Face Inference Providers (no local download; any served model)
lm = make_lm(LMConfig(engine="hf", model="meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct",
                      provider="auto"))         # or "hf-inference" / "together" / ...

# Local MLX (Apple Silicon) — needs `uv pip install mlx-lm` + a model
lm = make_lm(LMConfig(engine="local", model="mlx-community/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-4bit"))

for delta in lm.stream(build_messages("You are a receptionist.", [], "Hi there.")):
    print(delta, end="")
```

### HF Inference setup

- Auth: `hf auth login` once (token is read automatically), or set `HF_TOKEN`.
- `InferenceClient(provider="auto")` → unified **router** (OpenAI-compatible at
  `https://router.huggingface.co/v1/chat/completions`). `provider="auto"` picks a
  partner that serves the model; pin one for predictability.
- **Note:** the `hf-inference` provider itself now serves mostly CPU/small models
  (embeddings, classifiers, GPT-2-class). For conversational LLMs use
  `provider="auto"` (routes to Together/Fireworks/Cerebras/Novita/…). Free monthly
  credit then pay-as-you-go.

## Run

```bash
PY=~/Develop/mlx-audio/.venv/bin/python   # has huggingface_hub + mlx_audio (TTS)

$PY bench_lm.py                            # compare LM models: TTFT + tok/s
$PY demo_cascade.py --engine hf --model meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct \
     --user "Hi, I'd like to book an appointment for next week."
afplay cascade_reply.wav
```

## Measured on M5 Max (HF router LM + local Voxtral TTS)

| LM (router, provider=auto)        | TTFT   | tok/s |
| --------------------------------- | ------ | ----- |
| meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct | 439 ms | 34.1  |
| Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct          | 552 ms | 19.2  |
| Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct         | 620 ms | 14.0  |

End-to-end (`demo_cascade.py`, TTS warmed, clause-pipelined): **time-to-first-audio
≈ 1.5 s**, full short turn ≈ 3 s. The ~1.5 s is dominated by the LM round-trip
(network + provider TTFT ~0.5 s + first-clause generation) plus warm TTS synth
(~80–150 ms). A *local* LM would cut the network leg; PersonaPlex's full-duplex
path is ~160 ms by comparison. This is the core latency trade of the cascade.

## Mapping to the subaki-realtime (Tsubaki) app

The Python pieces translate directly to the Next.js/TS app:

- **LM call** → a server-side route (`app/api/llm/route.ts`) that calls the HF
  router OpenAI-compatible endpoint and **streams** the reply (SSE / ReadableStream).
  Keep the HF token server-side, exactly like the existing `xai`/`openai` token-mint
  routes. The browser never sees the token.
- **Switchable engine** → add `engine: "cascade-hf" | "cascade-local"` to the
  provider registry (`lib/data.ts`), and a per-persona LM `model`/`provider` +
  `system_prompt` (parallel to `xai-agent.ts` / `openai-agent.ts`).
- **STT** → Voxtral streaming (local `voxmlx`, or a hosted ASR provider) feeding
  the LM route; **TTS** → Voxtral TTS (local mlx-audio, or a hosted TTS) consuming
  the LM's streamed clauses via the same `clause_chunks` segmentation.
- **local ↔ HF switch** is just the `engine` field: `cascade-hf` hits the router;
  `cascade-local` points STT/LM/TTS at `localhost` MLX servers. The UI engine
  selector is unchanged.

## Files

- `cascade/lm.py` — swappable LM (`HFInferenceLM`, `LocalMlxLM`, `make_lm`).
- `cascade/tts.py` — Voxtral TTS wrapper + `clause_chunks` streaming segmenter.
- `demo_cascade.py` — end-to-end LM→TTS with latency instrumentation.
- `bench_lm.py` — compare LM models/providers (TTFT, tok/s).

# (1) Hugging Face Inference Providers — no local download; any *served* model
lm = make_lm(LMConfig(engine="hf", model="google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it",

### Which backend for which model

- **Served by an HF provider** (e.g. `google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it`) → `engine="hf"`.
- **Not served by any provider** (e.g. `Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` → BadRequest on the
  router; only GGUF/FP8 community quants exist) → run it locally and use
  `engine="openai"`. Check coverage at
  `https://huggingface.co/models?inference_provider=all`.

### Local llama-server (GGUF + MTP speculative decoding)

`llama-server` (llama.cpp) exposes an OpenAI-compatible `/v1` API, so `engine="openai"`
points straight at it. Recommended launch for the cascade — **text-only, MTP on,
thinking off, fixed port**:

```bash
llama-server \
  --model  models/gemma-4-12B/gemma-4-12B-it-qat-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf \
  --model-draft models/gemma-4-12B/mtp-gemma-4-12B-it.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 4 \
  -ngl 999 -fa on --jinja --port 8001 --alias unsloth/gemma-4-12b-it-qat-GGUF
```

**The two commands you may see — what differs:**

| aspect | `-hf …:UD-Q4_K_XL --spec-type draft-mtp` | `--model … --mmproj … --model-draft mtp-…gguf` |
| ------ | ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| weights | `-hf repo:quant` auto-downloads from HF | explicit local file paths (download yourself) |
| MTP draft | `--spec-type draft-mtp` selects the MTP algo (draft resolved by llama.cpp) | `--model-draft mtp-…gguf` points at the MTP head as an explicit draft file |
| vision | omitted → **text-only** | `--mmproj mmproj-F16.gguf` → loads the image encoder (gemma-4 is multimodal) |
| reasoning | default (off) | `--chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking":true}'` → **emits reasoning tokens first** |
| sampling / port | defaults, port 8080 | gemma's temp 1.0 / top-p 0.95 / top-k 64, port 8001 |

For a **low-latency voice receptionist** you want the leaner form: **no `--mmproj`**
(we only send text) and **thinking OFF** (reasoning tokens add seconds before the
first spoken word). `--spec-type draft-mtp` + `--model-draft <mtp.gguf>` and
`-hf …:quant` reach the same MTP speculative decoding — pick by whether you want
auto-download (`-hf`) or explicit local files. Both serve OpenAI-compatible `/v1`.

content.text:
Fully diagnosed and fixed — and it was **not** an availability problem.

## Why `gemma-4-31B-it` "failed"

It *is* served (the call succeeded). The catch: **gemma-4-31B-it is a reasoning model.** It streams its chain-of-thought in a separate `delta.reasoning` field and emits **zero spoken `delta.content`** until thinking finishes. With a small token budget it spent all 119 chunks reasoning (`content_chars=0, reasoning_chars=463, finish_reason="length"`). Our LM handler only forwards `content`, so it yielded nothing → `ttft` stayed `None` → the bench's `ttft * 1000` raised the misleading `TypeError`. So the "FAIL" was a thinking-budget issue surfacing as a crash, not a 4xx.

## The fix

A voice agent never speaks the chain-of-thought and wants low latency, so I added `LMConfig.enable_thinking` (**default `False`**), which sends `chat_template_kwargs:{enable_thinking:false}`:
- to the **HF router** via `extra_body` (verified harmless for non-reasoning models too),
- to **llama-server** via the request body (same as your `--chat-template-kwargs` flag).

Result: `gemma-4-31B-it` now answers directly — **TTFT 503ms, 15.2 tok/s**, end-to-end cascade **first-audio 1357ms** ("I can certainly help you with that. What day and time works best for you next week?"). I also made `bench_lm.py` report `WARN … no content (reasoning-only?)` instead of crashing, and added a `--think` flag to the demo for inspecting reasoning.

## Established router LM coverage

| model | TTFT | tok/s | note |
|---|---|---|---|
| meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct | 439ms | 34.1 | fastest |
| Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct | ~510ms | ~22 | |
| google/gemma-4-31B-it | 503ms | 15.2 | needs thinking off (now default) |
| google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it | 0.5–5s | 1.8–10 | MoE; provider-side queueing is variable |

Documented in the README (new "Reasoning models" section) and the main doc. The gemma-4-12B GGUF is still downloading (487M/7GB) for the live llama-server A/B — I'll pick that up when it lands. One small heads-up: `gemma-4-26B-A4B-it` showed very **variable** router latency (up to ~5s) — if you want a snappy hosted default, Llama-3.3-70B or gemma-4-31B-it are the steadier picks.

# Mistral Realtime Transcription: Basic Usage & Authentication

## Model and Audio Format

The documentation specifies using **`voxtral-mini-transcribe-realtime-2602`** as the realtime-capable model. Audio must be in **`pcm_s16le` encoding at 16000 Hz sample rate**.

## Basic Usage Pattern

The Python SDK example shows the core implementation:

```python
async for event in client.audio.realtime.transcribe_stream(
    audio_stream=audio_stream,
    model="voxtral-mini-transcribe-realtime-2602",
    audio_format=audio_format,
):
```

## Event Types Received

Transcription results arrive as event objects that the client handles:

- **`RealtimeTranscriptionSessionCreated`**: Session initialization
- **`TranscriptionStreamTextDelta`**: "Partial transcription updates" containing `event.text`
- **`TranscriptionStreamDone`**: Indicates completion
- **`RealtimeTranscriptionError`**: Error notifications

**Not explicitly documented in provided content.** The documentation shows initialization via `Mistral(api_key=REDACTED, server_url=args.base_url)` but does **not** specify:
- Exact WebSocket endpoint URL
- How the API key is transmitted (header vs. query parameter vs. message)
- Connection handshake protocol

The code abstracts these details within the SDK's `transcribe_stream()` method without exposing underlying connection mechanics.

## Target Delay Feature

Optional parameter `target_streaming_delay_ms=1000` enables context gathering before transcription begins, balancing speed versus accuracy.

I have the full picture now — including the exact line that answers your question. Let me lay it out.

## Why it "doesn't seem to need" auth headers — it does, the SDK just hides them

The docs example doesn't *show* you setting headers because the Python `Mistral(api_key=REDACTED client sets them **for you, inside the SDK**. Here's the actual handshake in `mistralai/extra/realtime/transcription.py`:

```python
# connect() resolves the API key into headers...
resolved_security = get_security_from_env(security, models.Security)
if resolved_security is not None:
    security_headers, security_query = get_security(resolved_security)
    headers |= security_headers          # → {"Authorization": "Bearer <MISTRAL_API_KEY>"}
...
websocket = await connect(               # websockets.asyncio.client.connect
    ws_url,
    additional_headers=dict(headers),    # ← the auth header IS set, on the WS handshake
    open_timeout=open_timeout,
    user_agent_header=user_agent,
)
```

So realtime transcription authenticates with an `Authorization: Bearer` **header on the WebSocket upgrade request**. That's the one thing that doesn't fit our browser-based system:

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The browser `WebSocket` constructor — `new WebSocket(url, protocols)` — **cannot set request headers**. There is no headers argument. So the browser physically cannot do what the Python SDK does.
- Our **xAI** engine connects the browser *directly* to `wss://api.x.ai/...` only because xAI issues a short-lived **ephemeral client-secret** we mint at `/api/xai/token` — passed in a way the browser can attach without headers. Mistral realtime has **no documented ephemeral-token or query-param auth** for this endpoint; it's bearer-header only.
- That's the whole mismatch. It's not the protocol (which is simple) — it's that the key must ride on a header the browser can't set.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## TypeScript SDK: can't help here

I checked `mistralai/client-ts` — it has **no realtime module at all** (no `transcribe_stream`, no `wss`, no `audio.realtime`). Realtime transcription exists **only in the Python SDK**. So "use the TS SDK instead of Python" isn't an option — we'd hand-roll the WS protocol either way. The good news: it's small and now fully pinned.

## The wire protocol (fully reverse-engineered, verbatim from the SDK)

- **URL:** `wss://api.mistral.ai/v1/audio/transcriptions/realtime?model=voxtral-mini-transcribe-realtime-2602`
- **Auth:** `Authorization: Bearer <MISTRAL_API_KEY>` header on handshake
- **Handshake:** server sends `{"type":"session.created", ...}` first — wait for it
- **Client → server** (JSON text frames):
  - `{"type":"session.update","session":{"audio_format":{"encoding":"pcm_s16le","sample_rate":16000},"target_streaming_delay_ms":1000}}`
  - `{"type":"input_audio.append","audio":"<base64 PCM, ≤262144 bytes decoded per frame>"}`
  - `{"type":"input_audio.flush"}` (force-emit) · `{"type":"input_audio.end"}` (stop)
- **Server → client** events: `transcription.text.delta` (→ `event.text`, partial) · `transcription.segment` · `transcription.language` · `transcription.done` (final) · `error`

This directly fixes your "stops before I finish talking" complaint: with realtime STT, **we** decide turn boundaries (via `target_streaming_delay_ms` + our own VAD/flush), not Chrome's aggressive Web Speech endpointer.

## The one decision: where the proxy lives

Since the browser can't set the header, the key must be attached server-side. The standard fix is a **server-side WS proxy**: browser ↔ our local WS (same-origin, no auth needed) ↔ Mistral (we add the bearer header), piping frames both ways. The `MISTRAL_API_KEY` never reaches the browser — same security posture as our token-mint routes.

The wrinkle: **Next.js 16 App Router has no WebSocket route handler**, so the proxy can't be a `route.ts`. Here's the fork:

End-to-end transcription validated — accurate streaming transcript through the proxy. Two facts confirmed for the client design: deltas are **incremental** (safe to accumulate), and `transcription.done` only fires after `input_audio.end` (so for multi-turn I keep the session open and use my own VAD for turn boundaries).

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Web Speech's "stops before I finish" is its fixed endpointer deciding your turn ended. With Mistral realtime, the model never decides turn boundaries — **we** do, via a client-side silence threshold we can tune (`SILENCE_HANGOVER_MS`). That's the core fix.
- The session stays open for the whole call; per-turn we send `input_audio.flush` (force-emit the tail) but never `input_audio.end` (that would close the stream). We pause *sending* audio while the assistant speaks so TTS isn't transcribed back.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

input.new_string:
The **MISTRAL** row runs a turn-based cascade instead of a single full-duplex
model: **Mistral realtime STT** → **`/api/llm`** (LM) → **`/api/mistral/tts`**
(Voxtral TTS). Per-persona backend/model/voice live in
`lib/realtime/cascade-agent.ts` (default LM `hf` + `google/gemma-4-31B-it`; voices
are Mistral slugs like `en_paul_neutral`):

```bash
# in fnox (run via `fnox exec -- bun run dev` / `mise run dev`)
HF_TOKEN=hf_...            # LM backend "hf"  (HF Inference router, any served model)
MISTRAL_API_KEY=...        # STT, TTS, and LM backend "mistral" (mistral-small-latest)
```

**Realtime STT needs a second process.** Mistral's realtime-transcription
endpoint (`voxtral-mini-transcribe-realtime-2602`) is a WebSocket that
authenticates with an `Authorization: Bearer` header on the handshake — and a
browser `WebSocket` cannot set request headers. So a tiny **bun WS proxy**
(`scripts/mistral-stt-proxy.ts`) sits between them: the browser connects to it
header-lessly, and it opens the authenticated upstream socket and pipes frames
both ways. `MISTRAL_API_KEY` never reaches the client.

```bash
mise run stt-proxy        # = fnox exec -- bun run scripts/mistral-stt-proxy.ts (:3001)
mise run stop-stt-proxy   # stop it (port STT_PROXY_PORT, default 3001)
```

The browser captures the mic at 16 kHz PCM16, streams it to the proxy, and turns
Mistral's `transcription.text.delta` events into user turns. Turn boundaries are
client-side: a tunable silence gate (`SILENCE_HANGOVER_MS` in
`lib/realtime/mistral-stt.ts`) decides when you've finished speaking — unlike the
browser's fixed endpointer, it won't cut you off mid-sentence. The proxy URL is
`NEXT_PUBLIC_MISTRAL_STT_WS` (default `ws://localhost:3001`). **If the proxy is
down or the mic is denied, STT automatically falls back to browser Web Speech**
(Chrome-only), so the cascade still works with just the dev server.

`/api/llm` streams an OpenAI-compatible chat completion from the chosen backend,
keeping the key server-side; HF reasoning models run with thinking off by default
(`chat_template_kwargs`, sent only to the HF backend — Mistral rejects it) so they
answer immediately. `/api/mistral/tts` returns per-clause MP3 from
`voxtral-mini-tts-2603`. Without `HF_TOKEN` the agent turn shows "— LM error —";
without `MISTRAL_API_KEY` TTS falls back to browser speechSynthesis.

Done. Here's where things landed.

## Answer to your question

The docs "don't need" auth headers only because the Python `Mistral(api_key=REDACTED SDK sets them **for you, inside `connect()`** — I found the exact line: `websockets.connect(ws_url, additional_headers={"Authorization": "Bearer …"})`. Realtime transcription authenticates with a **Bearer header on the WebSocket handshake**, and the browser `WebSocket` constructor literally cannot set request headers. That single fact — not the protocol — is what doesn't fit. (And the **TS SDK has no realtime module at all**; it's Python-only, so we hand-roll the protocol regardless.)

## What I built (standalone bun proxy, your pick)

- **`scripts/mistral-stt-proxy.ts`** — bun WS proxy on `:3001`. Browser connects header-lessly; it opens the authenticated upstream socket (`new WebSocket(url, { headers })` — the thing browsers lack) and pipes frames verbatim. `MISTRAL_API_KEY` never reaches the client. Run via `mise run stt-proxy` / `mise run stop-stt-proxy`.
- **`lib/realtime/mistral-stt.ts`** — `MistralStt` class: captures mic at 16 kHz PCM16, streams to the proxy, and converts `transcription.text.delta` events into turns. **Turn boundaries are ours** — a tunable silence gate (`SILENCE_HANGOVER_MS = 900`) decides when you've finished, directly fixing the "cut me off early" problem. `autoGainControl:false` keeps the VAD stable.
- **`use-cascade-session.ts`** — `MistralStt` is now the primary STT, with **automatic Web Speech fallback** if the proxy is down or the mic is denied. Mic pauses while the assistant speaks (TTS isn't transcribed back); the orb's input level now reflects real RMS.
- `mise.toml`, README, and `scripts/` excluded from `tsc`/oxlint (Bun globals); `scratchpad/` gitignored.

## Verified vs. needs your mic

- ✅ **Proxy → Mistral, end-to-end with real audio**: streamed a synthesized 16 kHz utterance through the proxy and got back the accurate streaming transcript (`session.created/updated` → `text.delta` → `transcription.done`). The Bearer-header bridge provably works.
- ✅ All four gates: `tsc`, `lint`, `fmt:check`, `build`.
- ⏳ **The in-browser mic loop** (capture → proxy → turn → LM → TTS) needs a human with a mic — I can't speak into it headlessly.

Found it. There's exactly one genuine **`[error]`** (msgid=8):

```
WebSocket connection to 'ws://localhost:3001/?model=voxtral-mini-transcribe-realtime-2602' failed:
Error in connection establishment: net::ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED
```

That's the one you saw. Here's the complete picture of everything printed:

| line | level | source | cause |
|---|---|---|---|
| `THREE.Clock … deprecated` | warn | **pre-existing** (WebGL Orb / R3F) | not from this change |
| `ScriptProcessorNode is deprecated` | warn | new — `mistral-stt.ts` mic capture | benign; the xAI engine already uses the same API |
| **`ws://localhost:3001 … ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED`** | **error** | new — STT tries to reach the proxy | **the proxy wasn't running** |

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The error is functionally harmless — our `onError` handler catches it and falls back to browser Web Speech (that's why the greeting still played). But Chrome logs **every** failed WebSocket handshake as a red console error at the network layer, and JS can't suppress it. So the real fix isn't in code — it's making sure the proxy is actually running. The footgun is that `mise run dev` and `mise run stt-proxy` were two separate commands, and the STT proxy is now required for the primary path.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

The clean fix: have `mise run dev` start the proxy automatically (backgrounded, and torn down when dev stops), so there's nothing to forget.

content.text:
## What the error was

The one genuine error:

```
WebSocket connection to 'ws://localhost:3001/?model=voxtral-mini-transcribe-realtime-2602'
failed: Error in connection establishment: net::ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED
```

**Cause:** the STT proxy wasn't running. `mise run dev` started only the Next dev server; the proxy was a separate `mise run stt-proxy`. When you pressed CALL on MISTRAL, the browser tried to open the STT WebSocket to `:3001`, nothing was there, and Chrome logged the refused handshake. It's **functionally harmless** — the engine catches it and falls back to browser Web Speech (the greeting still plays) — but the browser logs every failed WS handshake at the network layer and JS can't suppress it.

The other two lines are deprecation **warnings**, not errors:
- `THREE.Clock … deprecated` — pre-existing, from the WebGL Orb. Not mine.
- `ScriptProcessorNode is deprecated` — new, from the STT mic capture, but the xAI engine already uses the same API. Benign.

## The fix

`mise run dev` now starts the STT proxy in the background and tears it down when the server exits (`trap … EXIT`), so there's nothing to forget. **Verified live:** with the proxy up, the WebSocket connects, the greeting plays (`/api/llm` + `/api/mistral/tts` all 200), and the console shows **zero errors**.

Changes:
- [mise.toml](mise.toml) — `mise run dev` = proxy (backgrounded) + dev server, with cleanup trap
- [README.md](README.md) — documents the auto-start and what the refused-connection error means

Just run `mise run dev` and the cascade engine works end-to-end. If you ever want to run the proxy alone (or stop it), `mise run stt-proxy` / `mise run stop-stt-proxy` still exist.

content.text:
Voice reassignment done. Now the turn-detection problem.

## Why it doesn't detect when you finish

It's **not a lack of VAD** — there is one (an energy/silence gate in [mistral-stt.ts:152](lib/realtime/mistral-stt.ts:152)). The problem is what energy VAD always struggles with: the turn only ends after `SILENCE_HANGOVER_MS` of audio *below* `VOICE_RMS = 0.012`. That threshold is very low, so room tone, breathing, or mic self-noise keeps it reading "still speaking" and the silence timer never fills — the turn never closes. Tuning it per-mic is fragile, which is exactly why you're reaching for a manual control.

You're right that a manual turn button is the dependable answer for a half-duplex cascade. There are a few interaction models, and which one I build changes the UI — so let me confirm your preference:

questions.question: How do you want to mark the end of your turn in the cascade (STT→LM→TTS) engine?

options.label: Tap-to-talk toggle
options.description: Tap the mic to start your turn, tap again to send it. Hands-free between taps, works on desktop + mobile, no VAD guesswork. The mic button becomes a talk/send toggle while on the MISTRAL engine.

options.label: Hold-to-talk (push-to-talk)
options.description: Hold a button (and/or the Space key) while speaking, release to send. Most precise, but you must keep holding — awkward for long turns and less mobile-friendly.

options.label: Improved auto-VAD + manual send
options.description: Keep it hands-free: raise the threshold and add an adaptive noise floor so it auto-detects end-of-turn better, PLUS a 'send now' button to end the turn instantly when it lags. Best of both, but auto-detection is still imperfect in noisy rooms.

# @ricky0123/vad-web Overview

**What it is:**
A browser-based voice activity detector that runs client-side using machine learning. The documentation states it aims to provide "an accurate, user-friendly voice activity detector (VAD) that runs in the browser."

**How MicVAD works:**
The browser API detects speech segments and executes callbacks. You instantiate `MicVAD.new()` with configuration, then call `.start()` to begin monitoring audio from the user's microphone.

**Callbacks:**
The provided content explicitly mentions two callbacks:
- `onSpeechStart`: Triggered when speech begins
- `onSpeechEnd`: Receives audio data when speech ends

The callbacks `onFrameProcessed` and `onVADMisfire` are mentioned in your question but are not detailed in the provided content.

**onSpeechEnd return value:**

content.text:
Here's the key reframe: **VAD and STT are two separate jobs on the same mic audio.** Silero answers *"is this speech / did the turn end?"*; Mistral answers *"what words were said?"*. Right now we use Mistral for transcription and a crude energy gate for boundaries — and it's the energy gate that's failing. Silero replaces **only** the boundary detection; the Mistral streaming stays exactly as-is.

## Where it fits: in the browser, not a separate server

Silero is a ~2 MB ONNX model. In our TypeScript architecture it runs **client-side via ONNX Runtime Web (WASM/WebGPU)** — in the same place our broken RMS gate lives, inside `mistral-stt.ts`.

```
                    ┌───────────────── browser ─────────────────┐
   mic ─▶ AudioWorklet ─┬─▶ Silero VAD (ONNX-web) ─▶ onSpeechEnd ──┐   (boundary)
                        │                                          ▼
                        └─▶ PCM16 frames ──▶ WS proxy ──▶ Mistral ─▶ text  (transcript)
                    └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Why not a separate server?** That's the right shape only in your **Python/local-Voxtral path** (`~/Develop/voice-cascade`), where capture, VAD, and the model all live in one process and Silero runs in-process via torch/onnx. In the browser architecture a VAD server would be backwards: the audio is already in the browser, you want instant turn-end UI feedback, and routing audio out to a VAD service just to route the boundary back adds a hop and latency. (You *could* run Silero in the Node proxy via `onnxruntime-node`, but it buys nothing and delays the UI.)

## What changes in the codebase

`@ricky0123/vad-web` wraps Silero + ONNX Runtime Web + an AudioWorklet and emits `onSpeechStart` / `onSpeechEnd(Float32Array @16kHz)`. In `mistral-stt.ts` I'd:

- **Replace** the `ScriptProcessor` + RMS/adaptive-threshold block with a `MicVAD` instance (it also fixes the `ScriptProcessorNode` deprecation — it uses a proper AudioWorklet).
- `onFrameProcessed(frame)` → forward each frame to the Mistral proxy (`input_audio.append`) — **transcription pipeline unchanged**.
- `onSpeechEnd` → the robust turn-end trigger (flush + emit), replacing the silence timer. `redemptionFrames` becomes the tunable "let me finish" window.
- Keep the manual **Send** button and the Web Speech fallback.

**Tradeoff to confirm:** it pulls in `onnxruntime-web` (~a few MB of WASM) + the Silero model. By default vad-web loads those from a CDN (zero bundler config, good for dev); for self-hosting we'd drop the assets in `public/` and set `baseAssetPath`/`onnxWASMBasePath`.

Quote the exact strings used as ONNX input/output keys and the tensor shapes.

result.output:
# Silero V5 ONNX Inference Details

**Input Tensors:**
- `"input"`: Shape `[1, audioFrame.length]`, dtype float32 (audio samples)
- `"state"`: Shape `[2, 1, 128]`, dtype float32
- `"sr"`: Shape `[1]`, dtype int64, value `16000n`

**State Initialization:**
The state tensor is created with `"new ortInstance.Tensor("float32", zeroes, [2, 1, 128])"` where zeroes is an array of 384 elements.

**Output Tensors:**
- `"output"`: Contains speech probability (accessed via `.data[0]`)
- `"stateN"`: The updated state tensor for next inference

**Audio Frame Size:**
Variable length; the input shape dynamically uses `audioFrame.length` rather than a fixed sample count.

**State Reset:**
Calling `reset_state()` reinitializes `this._state = getNewState(this.ortInstance)`, creating a fresh zero-filled tensor.

**Key Inference Pattern:**
After each `session.run(inputs)` call, the returned `"stateN"` is stored to `this._state` for stateful processing across frames.

input.prompt: Describe the speech state machine: how positiveSpeechThreshold, negativeSpeechThreshold, redemptionFrames, minSpeechFrames, and preSpeechPadFrames are used to decide speech start and speech end. What are the default values of these options? Show the per-frame logic that increments redemption counters and decides onSpeechStart, onSpeechEnd, and misfire. Quote the defaults and the core conditional logic.

result.output:
# Speech State Machine Overview

## Default Values

```
positiveSpeechThreshold: 0.3
negativeSpeechThreshold: 0.25
redemptionMs: 1400
preSpeechPadMs: 800
minSpeechMs: 400
```

## State Machine Logic

The frame processor implements a hysteresis-based speech detector with grace period recovery:

**Speech Start Detection:**
When a frame's probability exceeds `positiveSpeechThreshold`, the system transitions to speaking state and fires `SpeechStart`. Then, after accumulating `minSpeechFrames` consecutive speech frames, it fires `SpeechRealStart`.

**Speech End Detection:**
When probability drops below `negativeSpeechThreshold`, a redemption counter increments. If this counter reaches `redemptionFrames` without detecting speech again, the system fires `SpeechEnd` (if minimum speech duration is met) or `VADMisfire` otherwise.

**Recovery Mechanism:**
If the VAD detects speech during the redemption period, it resets the counter to zero, treating the dip as a false negative.

**Pre-speech Padding:**
During non-speaking periods, the buffer maintains only the most recent `preSpeechPadFrames` worth of audio. This audio gets prepended to detected speech segments.

**Core Conditional:**
> "if (probs.isSpeech < this.options.negativeSpeechThreshold && this.speaking && 
++this.redemptionCounter >= this.redemptionFrames)"

This condition triggers speech end after sustained low probability values exceed the grace period.

Done — and verified on real audio in the actual browser.

## Where Silero fits (your question)

**In the browser, not a separate server.** Silero is just an ONNX model; it runs client-side via `onnxruntime-web` (WASM), right where the broken energy gate was. A separate VAD server is only the right shape for your **Python/local-Voxtral** path, where capture + VAD + model share one process. In the browser, the audio is already there and you want instant turn-end feedback — routing it out to a VAD service and back would only add latency.

**VAD ≠ STT.** Silero answers *"did they stop talking?"* (boundaries); Mistral answers *"what words?"* (transcript). Both read the same mic stream. I replaced **only** the boundary detection — Mistral streaming is untouched.

## What landed

- **`lib/realtime/silero-vad.ts`** — `SileroVad` class: dynamically imports `onnxruntime-web` (stays out of the server bundle), runs Silero v5 single-threaded, 512-sample/32 ms frames through a sequential inference queue, with a hysteresis state machine (`onSpeechStart`/`onSpeechEnd`).
- **`mistral-stt.ts`** — energy/RMS gate removed; each 2048-sample block is forwarded to Mistral *and* fed to Silero; `onSpeechEnd` ends the turn. RMS kept only for the orb meter. VAD-load failure is **non-fatal** (keeps Mistral + the Send button; no Web-Speech fallback).
- `onnxruntime-web@1.27.0` added; `public/silero_vad_v5.onnx` (2.3 MB) served by Next.
- Tunables in `mistral-stt.ts`: `VAD_REDEMPTION_MS` (900 — the "let me finish" window), `VAD_POSITIVE`/`VAD_NEGATIVE`, `VAD_MIN_SPEECH_MS`.

## Proof (headless, real audio)

- Model loads, ORT inits single-threaded, model fetched 200, **no fallback** (stayed in LISTENING).

Done. Here's what the version question turned up — it's more nuanced than a simple bump.

## What "v6.2.1" actually is

I checked the release: **v6.2.1 is a Python *packaging* change** — its entire changelog is *"make onnxruntime optional"*. The ONNX **interface is unchanged** from v5 (`input`/`state[2,1,128]`/`sr` → `output`/`stateN`). So there's no new model architecture to adopt.

Two traps I hit and resolved:

1. **The `check_vad_up_to_date.sh` script tracks the wrong file for us.** It compares against `files/silero_vad.onnx` — which is the **legacy 299 KB `h`/`c`-state model** (v4-style), *not* the model our `state`/`stateN` code uses. Following that script would have pointed at the old architecture.

2. **The current model needs a 64-sample context.** The real current model is `src/silero_vad/data/silero_vad.onnx`. It's the same graph as the model I was using but with **genuinely newer weights** (1.76M of 2.33M bytes differ). Dropping it in naively gave **maxProb 0.1 on clear speech** — because snakers4's current model uses the official convention of prepending a rolling **64-sample context** (input = 64 + 512 = 576). My earlier model was an export that took 512 directly. With the context added: **maxProb 1.0**, `onSpeechEnd` fires correctly.

## What changed

- **`public/silero_vad.onnx`** — now the current snakers4 model (replaces `silero_vad_v5.onnx`).
- **`silero-vad.ts`** — added the 64-sample rolling context (`CONTEXT_SAMPLES`), so `infer()` feeds 576 samples the official way; default model URL → `/silero_vad.onnx`.
- README + memory updated, with the `files/` vs `src/silero_vad/data/` distinction documented so this doesn't bite again.

**Verified live:** the app loads `/silero_vad.onnx`, ORT runs single-threaded, stays in LISTENING, no console errors; standalone inference on real speech gives maxProb 1.0 and fires end-of-turn correctly.

Both pinned CDN URLs serve the **exact same bytes** I validated (sha1 match). So the alternatives are real. Here's the landscape:

**Key context:** the app *already* loads the ORT WASM runtime (~10 MB) from jsDelivr at runtime — so it already requires network + trusts that CDN. That makes a few options sensible:

| Option | Repo binary? | Offline? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`public/`** (current) | yes (2.3 MB) | ✅ | Self-hosted, reproducible, same-origin. Idiomatic Next static asset. |
| **jsDelivr CDN, pinned** | **no** | ❌ | `cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/snakers4/silero-vad@v6.2.1/...` — verified identical bytes. Consistent with how we already load ORT WASM. |
| **Bundler import** (`new URL('./m.onnx', import.meta.url)`) under `lib/` | yes | ✅ | Out of `public/`, content-hashed + immutable-cached, co-located with code. Still a repo binary; minor Turbopack-config risk. |

A few things that are *not* great fits: an npm package (`@ricky0123/vad-web` ships a *different* model — the 512-direct export, which would undo the context fix), and HF Hub (works, but jsDelivr is simpler and we already use it).

My read: since we already CDN-load the ORT runtime, **pinning the model on jsDelivr** is the most consistent choice and gets the 2.3 MB binary out of the repo. The only thing it costs is offline support — which `public/` preserves. Which matters more to you?

# Tsubaki Design System — sync notes

## What this DS is
A hand-authored package (`design-system/`, pkg `tsubaki-ds`, global `TsubakiDS`)
distilled from the **claude.ai/design prototype** of the Tsubaki voice console
(project `70221de8…`), NOT from the Next.js app's `components/tsubaki/` (those
need Next runtime / WebGL / onnxruntime and don't render in the sandbox). The
package is plain React + a token-driven `src/styles.css`, so every component
renders standalone.

## Build / toolchain
- `cfg.buildCmd` = `bun run --cwd design-system build` → `tsc` emits `dist/` (JS + .d.ts). CSS is plain (`src/styles.css`), copied via `cssEntry`, not compiled.
- Converter entry: `--entry ./design-system/dist/index.js --node-modules design-system/node_modules`.
- **cfg paths are package-relative** (to `design-system/`), not config-home-relative: `srcDir: src`, `tsconfig: tsconfig.json`, `cssEntry: src/styles.css`. (Got bitten once — they were repo-relative and silently skipped → `[CSS_RUNTIME]`.)
- `cfg.provider` = `TsubakiRoot` — wraps every preview so tokens/theme apply.

## Render check without a download
No Playwright Chromium was installed in `.ds-sync`, but a build was already
cached at `~/Library/Caches/ms-playwright/chromium-1208` ("Google Chrome for
Testing", arm64). Reused it via the validator's `DS_CHROMIUM_PATH` env var, and
installed only the `playwright` JS package with `PLAYWRIGHT_SKIP_BROWSER_DOWNLOAD=1`:

```
export DS_CHROMIUM_PATH="$HOME/Library/Caches/ms-playwright/chromium-1208/chrome-mac-arm64/Google Chrome for Testing.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome for Testing"
```

Set this before `package-validate.mjs` / `package-capture.mjs` / `resync.mjs`.

## Known render warns (expected — not regressions)
- `[RENDER_BLANK]` **ChevGlyph**, **MicLineGlyph**, **StaticWaveform** — internal
  helpers used inside `MicSelector`; their floor cards are tiny by nature. Left
  unauthored on purpose.
- `[FONT_REMOTE]` "IBM Plex Mono", "Newsreader" — loaded via a Google Fonts
  `@import` at runtime by design (not shipped).

20 of 27 exports have authored previews (`.design-sync/previews/`), all graded
good. Floor cards (intentional): `Hr`, `Label`, `ScrollArea`, `TsubakiRoot`
(provider — renders empty), `ChevGlyph`, `MicLineGlyph`, `StaticWaveform`.
Authorable on any later re-sync.

## Re-sync risks (watch-list)
- **Grouping**: all cards land in the single `general` group (no per-component
  docs set a `category`). To group into Primitives/Icons/Visualizers/Domain,
  add `cfg.docsMap.<Name>` stubs (`---\ncategory: <Group>\n---`) or a `docsDir`.

- **Prototype drift**: this DS mirrors the prototype's components. If the
  prototype (or `lib/data.ts` shapes — `PersonaData`/`ProviderData`/`Tool`)
  changes, re-port into `design-system/src/` and rebuild.

# Tsubaki Design System

Brutalist/editorial **realtime voice console** design system — the component
library behind [Tsubaki](https://github.com/jessearmand/subaki-realtime). Plain
React + a token-driven `styles.css`, every component renders standalone (no Next
runtime, WebGL, or onnxruntime), distilled from the claude.ai/design prototype.

## Layout

```
design-system/      the package (pkg `tsubaki-ds`)
  src/              React components + styles.css (source of truth)
  dist/             tsc build output (gitignored)
  tsconfig.json     ES2020 + react-jsx, emits dist/ with .d.ts
.design-sync/       /design-sync skill config + previews + sync notes
  config.json       links to the claude.ai/design design-system project
  NOTES.md          toolchain + re-sync details — read before syncing
  previews/         per-component preview cards
```

`.design-sync/` and `design-system/` are siblings on purpose — `config.json`
paths are package-relative to `design-system/`. See `.design-sync/NOTES.md`.

## Build

```bash
bun install --cwd design-system
bun run --cwd design-system build      # tsc → design-system/dist
```

## Relationship to the app

The Tsubaki **app** (`~/Develop/realtime-persona`) is a separate repo and a
parallel port of the same prototype. This repo is the publishable design system
and the `/design-sync` source. If they drift, re-port the prototype into both.

### Configuring the cascade LM

The LM model isn't hard-coded — it's a catalog in **`config/lm-models.json`**, read
by both the server route (`app/api/llm`) and the client agent
(`lib/realtime/cascade-agent.ts`) via `lib/realtime/lm-config.ts`. No live model
list is fetched. To change the model every cascade persona uses, edit `default`:

```jsonc
{
  "default": "mistral-small",          // ← the active model id
  "backends": {
    "hf":      { "url": "https://router.huggingface.co/v1/chat/completions", "envKey": "HF_TOKEN",        "supportsThinking": true },
    "mistral": { "url": "https://api.mistral.ai/v1/chat/completions",        "envKey": "MISTRAL_API_KEY", "supportsThinking": false }
  },
  "models": [
    { "id": "gemma-4-31b", "label": "...", "backend": "hf",      "model": "google/gemma-4-31B-it", "temperature": 0.7, "maxTokens": 200 },
    { "id": "mistral-small", "label": "...", "backend": "mistral", "model": "mistral-small-latest", "temperature": 0.7, "maxTokens": 200 }
  ]
}
```

- **Add a model**: append to `models` (any model the backend serves — e.g. another
  HF-router repo) and point `default` at its `id`.
- **Add a backend**: add an entry to `backends` (OpenAI-compatible `url` + the
  `envKey` naming its fnox secret); reference it from a model's `backend`. The key
  value stays in fnox and is read server-side only — only the env var *name* and the
  public URL live in the file.
- **Per-persona override**: give a persona an `lmModelId` (a catalog id) in
  `cascade-agent.ts` to pin it to a different model than the global default.

Both pieces are committed:
- `d6b22b3` — the configurable LM catalog (`config/lm-models.json`)

## The picker

It renders exactly as you described — an inset row under each provider whose engine has a multi-model catalog. Today that's **only the cascade (MISTRAL) provider**; every other provider has a single fixed model, so they show **no inset** (driven by `lmModelsForEngine(engine)` — non-cascade returns `[]`, and the inset only renders when there's more than one model).

How it's wired:
- **`hooks/use-lm-model.ts`** — the selected catalog id, persisted to `localStorage` (`tsubaki.lm-model`), defaulting to the catalog's `default`.
- Threaded `lmModelId` through `app-shell → use-realtime-session → use-cascade-session → resolveCascadeAgent(persona, overrideModelId)`. **Precedence: runtime pick > a persona's `lmModelId` > catalog default.** Because `agentRef` updates every render, a switch applies on the **next turn** (you can even change it mid-call from the Providers tab).
- The chips `stopPropagation`, so picking a model doesn't also re-select the provider; the active chip uses the accent.

**Verified end-to-end:** selecting "Mistral Small" made `/api/llm` receive `{"backend":"mistral","model":"mistral-small-latest"}` and the greeting streamed from that model — not just a UI highlight.

One bug I caught and fixed along the way: I'd first put `display:flex` on the inset `<td>`, which drops it out of the table box model so `colSpan` was ignored and it shrank to ~535px. Moved the flex to an inner wrapper — the cell now spans the full row (confirmed 1216px → table edge).

All four gates pass. If you want, a natural follow-up is pushing this picker design back to the claude.ai/design prototype so the two stay in sync — but that's optional.

1	# PersonaPlex local inference on Apple Silicon (MLX)
2	
3	Status: **Phase 1 verified on hardware** — q8 is realtime on M5 Max (benchmarks below); live web server runs at `localhost:8998`. Remaining: subjective live-conversation notes (requires mic + headphones — the bundled client has no echo cancellation).
4	
5	## What we're running
6	
7	- **Model:** [nvidia/personaplex-7b-v1](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/personaplex-7b-v1) — full-duplex speech-to-speech (Moshi architecture, 8.37B params incl. depth transformer + Mimi codec), conditioned on a voice prompt (`NATF0-3`, `NATM0-3`, `VARF0-4`, `VARM0-4` presets) and a free-text persona prompt. Gated: auto-approve after accepting the NVIDIA Open Model License (account-level, do it once in the browser).
8	- **Runtime:** [mu-hashmi/personaplex-mlx](https://github.com/mu-hashmi/personaplex-mlx) — Python MLX port (moshi_mlx fork) with realtime web mode (`personaplex_mlx.local_web`), realtime terminal mode, and offline WAV mode. Quantizes the bf16 checkpoint at load time (`-q 4|8`).
9	- **Follow-up checkpoint (Phase 2):** [kyutai/personaplex-rl-seamless](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/personaplex-rl-seamless) — RL fine-tune for turn-taking/backchanneling. Gated, bf16 only, RL delta licensed CC BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial).
10	
11	## Setup (commands that worked)
12	
13	```bash
14	git clone https://github.com/mu-hashmi/personaplex-mlx ~/Develop/personaplex-mlx
15	cd ~/Develop/personaplex-mlx
16	uv venv --python 3.12 .venv
17	uv pip install -e . --python .venv/bin/python
18	
19	# one-time: accept the license at https://huggingface.co/nvidia/personaplex-7b-v1
20	hf download nvidia/personaplex-7b-v1   # ~17GB model.safetensors + tokenizer + mimi + voices.tgz + dist.tgz
21	
22	.venv/bin/python -m personaplex_mlx.local_web -q 8 \
23	  --voice NATF2 \
24	  --text-prompt "You enjoy having a good conversation."
25	# web client + WebSocket at http://localhost:8998
26	```
27	
28	Notes:
29	
30	- `-q 8` quantizes in-process from bf16 (no pre-quantized `model.q8.safetensors` exists in the NVIDIA repo). Community benchmarks of the Swift MLX build report 4-bit produces garbled output; prefer 8-bit or bf16.
31	- The bundled web client has **no echo cancellation** — use headphones.
32	- Quantization at load is cheap (~2s total to load + quantize on M5 Max), so there's no need to persist quantized weights.
33	- Benchmark harness: `bench_steps.py` in the fork checkout (`~/Develop/personaplex-mlx`); response audio samples: `bench-output-q8.wav` / `bench-output-bf16.wav` there.
34	
35	## Phase 2: kyutai RL checkpoint (done — 2026-06-18)
36	
37	`kyutai/personaplex-rl-seamless` is gated **auto** and its file layout is identical to base (`model.safetensors`, same Mimi checkpoint, tokenizer, `voices.tgz` — same 18 NATF/NATM/VARF/VARM voices). License accepted on account jessearmand. Runs via the same server:
38	
39	```bash
40	.venv/bin/python -m personaplex_mlx.local_web -q 8 --hf-repo kyutai/personaplex-rl-seamless ...
41	```
42	
43	**One code fix was required.** Unlike base (whose `config.json` is a stub with no `dim`, routing to the hardcoded `config_personaplex_7b_v1()`), the RL repo ships a *full* `config.json`, so the fork parses it via `LmConfig.from_config_dict` — which had two bugs: it hardcoded the feed-forward width as `4 * dim` (PersonaPlex uses `hidden_scale = 4.125`, so weights wouldn't match) and passed `depformer_dim_feedforward` straight through (it's `null` in the RL config → `TypeError`). Fixed `from_config_dict` in `personaplex_mlx/models/lm.py` to honor `hidden_scale` (default 4) for both the main and depformer feed-forward dims. After the fix the RL model loads and runs realtime at q8: **67.3 ms/step mean, p95 70.2 ms, RTF 0.84, 10.1 GB** (≈3 ms/step slower than base, still comfortably realtime).
44	
45	### A/B vs base — greeting cadence is unchanged
46	
47	RL-seamless is RL-tuned for **interaction dynamics** (pause handling, turn-taking, backchanneling, user interruption), *not* solo-monologue fluency. Confirmed by an opening-greeting cadence A/B (voiced fraction of the first 3 s, silence mic, 3 seeds each via `scratchpad/cadence.py`):
48	
49	| model | medical greeting (voiced %, 3 seeds) |
50	| ----- | ------------------------------------ |
51	| base `nvidia/personaplex-7b-v1` | 63 / 56 / 75 (avg ~65%) |
52	| RL `kyutai/personaplex-rl-seamless` | 68 / 64 / 62 (avg ~65%) |
53	
54	Statistically identical — **RL does not fix the halting/choppy opening greeting** (that cadence is inherent to the architecture's solo speech rhythm, and is already faithfully reproduced; see the residual-glitch section). RL's benefit appears only in live conversation (turn-taking, fewer mid-greeting/mid-turn self-interruptions), which the headless silence probes can't exercise — evaluate it in the browser. The mic-gate already covers the greeting-interruption case for both checkpoints.
55	
56	A user recording of a full RL conversation (`astronaut_conversation.webm`, 5m39s) confirms it: onset 0.29s but only ~1% voiced in the first 3s — the opening is tiny fragments (70–360ms) then a 3.6s wait, **zero clicks** (max sample step 0.103). Same halting cadence as base, no codec artifact.
57	
58	### Why the halting cadence is inherent to the architecture
59	
60	The "glitch" is the model's *speaking rhythm*, and it falls out of how Moshi/PersonaPlex generates — it is not a bug we can tune away in the serving stack:
61	
62	1. **Frame-synchronous streaming at 12.5 Hz with an "inner monologue."** Every 80 ms the model jointly samples **one text token** — an inner-monologue word-piece, *or* a `PAD`/`EPAD` token (ids 0–3) meaning "emit no word this frame" — together with the matching Mimi audio codebooks (`delays=[0,0,1,1,…]` is the text→audio acoustic offset). Speech only comes out on frames where the text stream emits a real word-piece; between word-pieces it emits `PAD` and the audio is silence/breath. So speech is *intrinsically* delivered in word/syllable-sized bursts separated by pad-driven gaps — **the 50–360 ms "gaps" we measure are `PAD` runs in the inner monologue, not dropped audio.**
63	
64	2. **No utterance-level prosody planning.** To stay ready to yield to the user at any 80 ms frame (full-duplex), the model commits token-by-token with no look-ahead over the whole sentence. A non-streaming TTS plans a smooth pitch/timing contour across the entire utterance; Moshi decides "speak or pad" and "which word-piece" one frame at a time under temperature sampling. That yields choppier, less-planned timing — most pronounced at turn onset, before the model "gets going."
65	
66	3. **Trained on natural two-person dialogue.** The data is real conversational speech — hesitations, variable pacing, mid-sentence pauses — not the polished read-aloud prosody of TTS corpora. The model faithfully reproduces that disfluent, conversational cadence rather than narration smoothness.
67	
68	4. **It's the price of full-duplex.** The very mechanism that lets the model listen and barge-in at 80 ms granularity (per-frame speak/pad decision, no look-ahead) is what makes its monologue halting. One autoregressive stream can't be both narration-smooth *and* 80 ms-responsive. RL-seamless tunes *when* to pad/yield in response to the user (turn-taking); the *within-turn* word-by-word delivery is structural — hence unchanged in the A/B above.
69	
70	**Implication:** smoothing the opening would require a different model class (a non-streaming TTS for the greeting, or a half-duplex turn-based model that plans whole utterances), not a fix to PersonaPlex serving. Within PersonaPlex the levers are marginal — lower audio-sampling temperature, voice-prompt choice, or simply accepting it as the model's conversational voice. This is the main reason to evaluate alternatives like Voxtral (below).
71	
72	## Measurements
73	
74	Hardware: **Apple M5 Max, 64GB unified memory**. Benchmark: `bench_steps.py` in the fork's checkout — mirrors the offline generation loop (mimi encode + LM step + mimi decode per 80ms frame) over a 10.6s/133-step input, timed per step (first 2 warmup steps excluded), voice `NATF2`.
75	
76	| Config | ms/step mean (budget 80ms) | p95  | max  | RTF  | Peak memory | Load time |
77	| ------ | -------------------------- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ----------- | --------- |
78	| q8     | 64.0                       | 65.9 | 67.4 | 0.80 | 10.1 GB     | 1.7s + 1.1s prompts |
79	| bf16   | 78.7                       | 80.9 | 83.2 | 0.98 | 15.9 GB     | 1.2s + 1.2s prompts |
80	
81	- q8 is **realtime with ~20% headroom** — p95 well under the 80ms frame budget, very low jitter (max 67.4ms).
82	- bf16 is **not reliably realtime** (p95 crosses the 80ms budget) — use q8. This also means the bandwidth-bound 7B temporal transformer is the bottleneck, so the q8 headroom is genuine, not load-order luck.
83	- End-to-end response latency (by ear):
84	- Barge-in / interruption behavior:
85	- Voice preset notes:

87	## Protocol (verified in source — basis for the future Tsubaki engine)
88	
89	WebSocket at `ws://localhost:8998/api/chat`. Binary frames, first byte is the message tag:
90	
91	| Tag    | Meaning                                              |
92	| ------ | ---------------------------------------------------- |
93	| `0x00` | handshake                                            |
94	| `0x01` | audio — continuous **Ogg Opus** stream (24kHz mono), both directions |
95	| `0x02` | text token (agent transcript)                        |
96	| `0x06` | ping                                                 |
97	
98	Session config travels as **URL query params** on connect: `text_prompt`, `voice_prompt` (e.g. `NATF2.pt`), temperatures, top-k, seeds, repetition penalty. Mimi codec frames are 80ms (12.5Hz) — each model step must complete in ≤80ms for realtime.
99	
100	## Review
101	
102	First impression, I can see the default voice greeting that the model is outputting, but the voice or speech couldn't be heard clearly. It can be about the codec, it can be about thhe MLX inference itself. I couldn't test further because the speech itself is not being played back correctly
103	
104	### Diagnosis (2026-06-13)
105	
106	Investigated the full path: MLX inference → Mimi decode → `sphn` Opus encode → WebSocket → browser `opus-recorder` decode → `moshi-processor` AudioWorklet. **The audio pipeline is correct end to end — the greeting is clean, normal-level, intelligible speech, and the browser reproduces it faithfully.** Evidence:
107	
108	1. **Inference** — offline q8/bf16 produce coherent audio and text (`bench-output-q8.wav`).
109	2. **Opus codec is transparent** — a controlled 200 Hz tone round-trips through `sphn.OpusStreamWriter(24000)` at 1.00s→1.00s; ffmpeg/libopus (what the browser uses) agrees. The `OpusHead` declares `input_sample_rate=48000`, which is *normal* per RFC 7845 (informational only; decoders always run at 48 kHz internally) — it is **not** a bug.
110	3. **Browser playback is faithful** — captured the raw server Opus *and* the decoded frames fed to the playback worklet **in the same session** (browser instrumented via chrome-devtools). Played-vs-server duration ratio = **1.008**, pitch identical (**86.5 Hz** both). No 2× inflation, no sample-rate error. (An earlier "2× / lower-pitch" read was an artifact of comparing two *different* stochastic sessions — each connect uses a fresh seed and greets differently.)
111	4. **Streaming audio is spectrally clean** — spectral flatness 0.006–0.053 (tonal/harmonic speech; garbled noise would be >0.3). Levels match the known-good offline output (loudest-1s RMS 0.097 vs 0.099).
112	
113	**So the in-browser "can't be heard clearly" is not inference, codec, or sample-rate.** Confirmed by the user: `afplay ws-greeting.wav` is perfectly clear, and the browser greeting stays mangled even on AirPods Pro 2 with noise cancellation — so it is **not** echo/feedback either (the earlier echo hypothesis is retracted).
114	
115	### Root cause (proven at the speaker output)
116	
117	Instrumented the live page to capture, in the same session, both the audio frames *delivered into* the playback worklet and the audio it *outputs to the speakers* (ScriptProcessor tap on the worklet node):
118	
119	| Tap | duration | peak | rms | silence |
120	| --- | -------- | ---- | --- | ------- |
121	| delivered → worklet | 17.44s | 0.316 | 0.0155 | — |
122	| worklet → speakers  | 17.92s | 0.160 | 0.0032 | **98% of frames** |
123	
124	The worklet receives clean, full-level audio but emits ~98% silence at roughly half the peak and a fifth of the RMS. Cause: **the server streams the opening greeting as a ~2× realtime burst** (`send_loop` ships decoded PCM as fast as it's produced, with no realtime pacing; the model runs at RTF ~0.8 and isn't gated by mic input at connect). The bundled client's barebones `moshi-processor` AudioWorklet has only an ~80–240 ms jitter buffer (observed startup `delay` peaked at **2.24s**); it cannot absorb a multi-second burst, so its overflow-drop + glitch-fade path collapses to near-silence. Hence: clean via `afplay` (no worklet), mangled in-browser, unaffected by headphones/NC.
125	
126	This is a limitation of the bundled barebones web client, **not** the model or the serving stack.
127	
128	### Mitigations
129	
130	- For evaluation, audition greetings headlessly (bypasses the worklet) — see samples below.
131	- For the bundled client specifically, the real fix is server-side realtime pacing of `send_loop` and/or a larger client jitter buffer; not worth patching since we won't ship that client.
132	- **Tsubaki engine:** `use-moshi-session.ts` owns its own playback (reuse `PlaybackQueue` from `xai-audio.ts`) and mic capture, so it gets a properly sized jitter buffer, output gain, and `echoCancellation: true` constraints for free — the burst-collapse cannot happen there.
133	
134	### Greeting samples (headless, clean) — `afplay ~/Develop/personaplex-mlx/greet-<name>.wav`
135	
136	Generated via `greetings_batch.sh` (per-connection `voice_prompt`/`text_prompt` query params against the running server; no restart needed):
137	
138	| name | voice | transcript |
139	| ---- | ----- | ---------- |
140	| medical | NATF2 | "Good morning, you're calling Dr. Jones's medical office. How can I help today?" |
141	| bank | NATF1 | "Thank you for calling First Neuron Bank. How can I help today?" |
142	| concierge | NATF3 | "Hello, this is Tsubaki speaking. How can I assist you today?" |
143	| astronaut | NATM0 | "Hello, this is Alex." (discussion personas expect a human first; less monologue from silence) |
144	
145	Note: with silence-only input the model gives a natural phone greeting then waits for the caller — service personas (medical/bank/concierge) yield the most natural multi-clause openings. The `text:` token stream shows minor display artifacts (e.g. "you'" for "you're"); the audio is correct.
146	
147	Diagnostic harnesses (in `~/Develop/personaplex-mlx`): `ws_probe.py` (headless WS client → decodes server greeting to WAV; `--dump-opus` for the raw stream), `bench_steps.py`, `greetings_batch.sh`.
148	
149	### Fix applied (2026-06-15)
150	
151	Two server-side changes landed in `personaplex-mlx`:
152	
153	1. **Realtime output pacing** (user commit `e41bf5a`, `OutboundAudioPacer`) — releases decoded PCM at realtime cadence instead of bursting, plus an in-memory patch that enlarges the bundled worklet's jitter buffer (80→320 ms initial, max 1200 ms). Killed the 2× **overflow** burst above, but exposed an **underrun**.
154	2. **`model_loop` yield + startup warmup** (`local_web.py`) — `await asyncio.sleep(0)` between MLX steps so the paced `send_loop` is never starved while draining a startup backlog (was a ~460 ms event-loop stall → worklet underrun → crackle), plus a `ServerState.warmup()` that pre-compiles the sampling graph so the first session doesn't compile-stall.
155	
156	Verified: server delivery stalls >120 ms went 2→0 (gaps now 80–100 ms from the first frame, real-speech input included); browser worklet output went from 98 %-silence to faithfully matching its input (peak 0.316, **0 discontinuities**). Probes: `scratchpad/gap_timeline2.py`, `convo_probe.py`.
157	
158	### Residual "glitch": full-duplex self-interruption (not a pipeline bug)
159	
160	After the fix, a user recording of a live "Bank" conversation (`bank_teller_personaplex_audio.webm`) still had a choppy opening: silence dropouts of ~1120 ms and ~860 ms in the first ~2.7 s, then clean. But the recording has **zero clicks** (max sample step 0.032) — these are clean silence gaps, not codec/buffer artifacts. Tracing it:
161	
162	- Server delivery under real-speech mic input is **smooth** (p95 84 ms, no gaps >120 ms) — so the dropouts are **not** produced on the wire.
163	- With **pure-silence** mic, the greeting is **continuous** (onset 0.22 s → 3.52 s, no internal gaps).
164	- Feeding low-level mic **noise** reproduces the dropouts: at −40 dB an internal 300 ms gap appears and the greeting is cut short; at higher levels it truncates further.
165	
166	**Conclusion:** the full-duplex model pauses/cuts its own greeting whenever it detects mic activity. The bundled client requests `echoCancellation:true, noiseSuppression:true, autoGainControl:true`, but **AGC boosts ambient room noise/breathing** during the silent greeting window enough to trip the model's turn-taking — even on AirPods (no real echo). This is model behavior, not the codec/pacing/buffer path.
167	
168	Mitigations (for the future Tsubaki engine, which owns mic capture):
169	- **Gate the mic during the opening greeting** — withhold mic frames (or hard-gate below a VAD threshold) until the model finishes greeting / the user clearly speaks. Simplest, most effective.
170	- Disable `autoGainControl` (keep `echoCancellation`/`noiseSuppression`) so ambient noise isn't amplified into false speech.
171	- The RL checkpoint `kyutai/personaplex-rl-seamless` specifically targets "inappropriate interruptions" and should be less twitchy here — worth A/B-ing in Phase 2.
172	
173	Probes for this: `scratchpad/silence_greeting.py`, `noise_greeting.py`, `convo_probe.py`.
174	
175	### Mic-gate prototype (2026-06-15) — implemented & validated
176	
177	Prototyped the mic-gate **server-side** in `personaplex-mlx` (cleaner than patching minified client JS; the server directly controls model input):
178	
179	- `personaplex_mlx/greeting_gate.py` — `GreetingGate`: starts muted, feeds the model silence; observes the model's decoded **output** and opens once it has produced voiced audio and then `end_silence_ms` of quiet (greeting turn over), with a `max_ms` safety cap. Sample-count based (no wall clock) → deterministic, unit-tested (`tests/test_greeting_gate.py`).
180	- `local_web.py` — instantiated per session; `recv_loop` replaces mic frames with silence while `is_muted()`, `send_loop` calls `observe_output()`. On by default; flags `--no-greeting-gate`, `--greeting-gate-{rms,end-ms,max-ms}` (defaults 0.02 / 600 / 12000).
181	
182	Validated against the same noise that previously chopped the greeting — same prompt/seed, gate ON, varying only mic level:
183	
184	| mic level | greeting (gate ON) | greeting (gate OFF, prior) |
185	| --------- | ------------------ | -------------------------- |
186	| 0.0 silence | continuous 0.22→3.76s | continuous →3.52s |
187	| 0.03 noise | continuous 0.22→**3.76s** | truncated →2.9s |
188	| 0.08 loud noise | continuous 0.22→**3.76s** | (worse) |
189	
190	The greeting is now identical regardless of mic noise, and an end-to-end probe (`scratchpad/gate_e2e.py`) confirms the gate **opens after the greeting** so the model responds to subsequent user speech. Gates pass: `ruff format`/`check`, `ty`, 11 tests. The browser receives the gated (clean) greeting unchanged, since the gate is upstream of Opus/WS. Next: port the same logic into `use-moshi-session.ts` (client-side, plus `autoGainControl:false`).
191	
192	## mlx-audio evaluation (`~/Develop/mlx-audio`) — considered, not adopted
193	
194	Checked whether [mlx-audio](https://github.com/Blaizzy/mlx-audio) (Blaizzy, MIT, actively maintained) can replace or augment our stack. **We do not use it anywhere** (neither `personaplex-mlx` nor `realtime-persona` reference it; our codec path is `rustymimi` + `sphn`). Findings:
195	
196	- It has a **pure-MLX Mimi codec** and a **full-duplex Moshi STS** (`sts/models/moshi/`, `generate()` accepts user-mic audio, warms its tokenizer) — but it's **base `moshiko` only**, with **zero PersonaPlex/NVIDIA awareness** (no voice-prompt `.pt` injection, no text-persona `step_system_prompts`, no `config_personaplex_7b_v1`). It cannot run PersonaPlex without porting all the persona conditioning our fork already implements.
197	- Its server's `/v1/realtime` WebSocket is **STT-only** (OpenAI-Realtime *transcription* — no speech output); there's no full-duplex STS browser server, so it doesn't solve the web-serving problem `local_web.py` does.
198	- Its realtime code independently documents the **same MLX+asyncio constraint** we hit ("MLX streams are thread-bound… all realtime MLX work must share one thread"), serialized via an inference lock — confirming the event-loop-blocking root cause behind the greeting crackle was intrinsic, not a fork bug.
199	
200	**Verdict:** keep `personaplex-mlx` for PersonaPlex full-duplex; do **not** migrate the codec. Revisit mlx-audio only if/when Tsubaki wants **non-duplex local engines** (local TTS like Kokoro/Sesame, or local STT like Parakeet/Whisper) — its OpenAI-compatible API would map cleanly onto the existing token-mint/engine patterns.
201	
202	## Voxtral evaluation (`~/Develop/voxmlx`) — STT leg of a cascade alternative (2026-06-18)
203	
204	[Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime-2602](https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime-2602) (Mistral, **Apache-2.0**) run via [awni/voxmlx](https://github.com/awni/voxmlx). **Crucial: this is streaming ASR — audio in, *text* out. It does not generate speech.** ≈3.4B LM + ≈970M causal audio encoder, natively streaming (sliding-window attention, <500 ms claimed delay), 16 kHz mono input, 13 languages.
205	
206	Setup + benchmark on **M5 Max**:
207	
208	```bash
209	git clone https://github.com/awni/voxmlx ~/Develop/voxmlx && cd ~/Develop/voxmlx
210	uv venv --python 3.12 .venv && uv pip install -e . --python .venv/bin/python
211	.venv/bin/voxmlx --audio file.flac          # file mode (soundfile-readable: flac/16k wav)
212	.venv/bin/voxmlx                            # mic streaming
213	```
214	
215	Default model `mlx-community/Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime-6bit`. Results (offline batch, `scratchpad/bench_vox.py`): **RTF 0.091 (~11× realtime), 4.2 GB peak, 0.6 s load**, transcription verbatim-accurate on a 10.6 s clip. (A non-16k/flac WAV failed `soundfile.read`; convert with ffmpeg to `-ac 1 -ar 16000` flac first.) The <500 ms figure is the streaming-mode incremental delay (design-bound, not compute-bound — compute has 10× headroom).
216	
217	### Where Voxtral fits: full-duplex vs cascade
218	
219	Voxtral is **not** a PersonaPlex replacement — it's the STT front-end of a **cascade voice agent** (Voxtral STT → LLM → TTS). The two architectures trade off exactly along the cadence axis above:
220	
221	| | PersonaPlex (full-duplex S2S) | Cascade (Voxtral STT → LLM → TTS) |
222	| --- | ----------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
223	| Assistant voice | model generates it directly | a TTS generates it |
224	| Opening/utterance cadence | **halting** (per-frame speak/pad, no look-ahead) | **smooth** (TTS plans whole utterance) |
225	| Turn-taking / barge-in | native, 80 ms granularity | turn-based; barge-in must be engineered (VAD + cancel) |
226	| Latency | ~160 ms model delay, one model | STT delay + LLM TTFT + TTS first-chunk (additive) |
227	| Voice/persona control | voice-prompt `.pt` + text prompt | full control (any TTS voice + system prompt) |
228	| Local cost on M5 Max | q8 ~10.1 GB, RTF 0.84 | Voxtral 4.2 GB RTF 0.09 + LLM + TTS (all fit in 64 GB) |
229	
230	So the cascade is the path to **smooth assistant speech** (no halting greeting) at the cost of true full-duplex naturalness and additive latency. Voxtral's tiny footprint (4.2 GB, RTF 0.09) leaves ample room for a local LLM + a local TTS on the same machine.
231	
232	### Voxtral TTS — the speech-generation leg (2026-06-18)
233	
234	[Voxtral-4B-TTS-2603](https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Voxtral-4B-TTS-2603) (Mistral; **CC-BY-NC-4.0**, non-commercial) runs locally via **mlx-audio** (`voxtral_tts` model) using the `mlx-community/Voxtral-4B-TTS-2603-mlx-6bit` quant. 1016 M params, 24 kHz output, **20 preset voices** across 9 languages (`casual_male`, `cheerful_female`, `neutral_male`, `fr_female`, …; no voice cloning).
235	
236	Setup + benchmark on **M5 Max**:
237	
238	```bash
239	cd ~/Develop/mlx-audio && uv venv --python 3.12 .venv
240	uv pip install -e . "mistral-common[audio]" soundfile --python .venv/bin/python
241	# from mlx_audio.tts.utils import load; model = load("mlx-community/Voxtral-4B-TTS-2603-mlx-6bit")
242	# model.generate(text=..., voice="cheerful_female", stream=True, streaming_interval=0.08)
243	```
244	
245	Results (`scratchpad/bench_tts.py`, `ttfa.py`): **RTF 0.25–0.42, 4.0 GB peak, 3.0 s load**, coherent multilingual speech. Crucially for a cascade, it **streams**: warm **time-to-first-audio ≈ 80–150 ms** (at `streaming_interval=0.08–0.5`; the first cold call is ~1 s due to graph compile). At `temperature=0.8` sentence-boundary pauses can run long (a 1.4 s inter-sentence gap in one take) — `temperature≈0.5` tightens it. Samples staged at `~/Develop/mlx-audio/voxtral_tts_medical*.wav`.
246	
247	**Both cascade legs now validated locally:** Voxtral STT (4.2 GB, RTF 0.09, <500 ms streaming) + Voxtral TTS (4.0 GB, RTF ≤0.42, TTFA ~80–150 ms) ≈ **8 GB combined**, leaving room for a local LLM in 64 GB — and the whole cascade can run alongside or instead of PersonaPlex (10.1 GB). Whether the TTS actually *sounds* smoother than PersonaPlex's halting opening is a by-ear judgment (the voiced-fraction metric, 45–68 %, overlaps PersonaPlex and can't distinguish planned-TTS prosody from per-frame halting) — but a TTS plans whole utterances, which is the structural reason to expect smoother delivery. License caveat: TTS is **CC-BY-NC** (non-commercial), same constraint as RL-seamless.
248	
249	**Open next step for the cascade:** ~~wire Voxtral STT → LLM → Voxtral TTS and measure end-to-end latency~~ — done (below). Remaining: engineer barge-in (VAD + TTS cancel) since the cascade is turn-based, and a live Voxtral streaming/mic test.
250	
251	### Cascade LM stage + end-to-end latency (2026-06-19)
252	
253	Prototyped the **LM → TTS** half of the cascade with a **swappable LM** at `~/Develop/voice-cascade/` (Python; runs in the mlx-audio venv). The LM stage (`cascade/lm.py`) has one streaming interface with two backends, selected by `LMConfig.engine` — mirroring Tsubaki's `provider.engine` switch:
254	
255	- **`engine="hf"`** — any chat model on the Hub via **Hugging Face Inference Providers**. `huggingface_hub.InferenceClient(provider="auto")` hits the unified **router** (OpenAI-compatible, `https://router.huggingface.co/v1/chat/completions`); token from `hf auth login`/`HF_TOKEN`, no local download. (The `hf-inference` provider itself now serves mostly CPU/small models — embeddings, GPT-2-class; for conversational LLMs use `provider="auto"`, which routes to partner providers.)
256	- **`engine="openai"`** — any **OpenAI-compatible** `/v1` endpoint via httpx+SSE: a local **`llama-server`** (llama.cpp, GGUF + MTP speculative decoding), vLLM, etc. The difference from the HF path is just `base_url`. This is the path for models **no provider serves** (e.g. `Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` → BadRequest on the router; only GGUF/FP8 quants exist).
257	- **`engine="local"`** — local MLX via `mlx-lm` (written, untested — needs a model download).
258	
259	Router LM results (M5 Max client, `bench_lm.py`, `provider="auto"`):
260	
261	| model | TTFT | tok/s | served? |
262	| ----- | ---- | ----- | ------- |
263	| meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct | 439 ms | 34.1 | ✅ router |
264	| Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct | ~510 ms | ~22 | ✅ router |
265	| google/gemma-4-31B-it | 503 ms | 15.2 | ✅ router (needs thinking off) |
266	| google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it | 0.5–5 s (variable) | 1.8–10 | ✅ router (MoE; provider-side queueing) |
267	| Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | — | — | ❌ no provider → local llama-server |
268	
269	**Reasoning-model gotcha (found via `gemma-4-31B-it`):** it streams chain-of-thought in a `reasoning` delta field and emits **no spoken `content`** until thinking ends, so a small token budget yields zero output (looks like a failure — a `TypeError` in the bench, not a 4xx). Fix: `LMConfig.enable_thinking=False` (default), which sends `chat_template_kwargs:{enable_thinking:false}` to the router (`extra_body`) and llama-server (body) — ignored by non-reasoning models. A voice agent never speaks the CoT and wants low latency, so thinking stays off. With it off, `gemma-4-31B-it` → TTFT 503 ms.
270	
271	End-to-end cascade → Voxtral TTS: `gemma-4-31B-it` **TTFT 503 ms, first-audio 1357 ms**; `gemma-4-26B-A4B-it` first-audio 1187 ms (when the provider is warm). Local llama-server path (gemma-4-12B-it-qat GGUF + MTP) wired via `engine="openai"`.
272	
273	End-to-end **LM → clause-segmented → Voxtral TTS** (`demo_cascade.py`, TTS warmed): **time-to-first-audio ≈ 1.5 s**, full short turn ≈ 3 s. Dominated by the LM round-trip (network + provider TTFT ~0.5 s + first-clause generation) plus warm TTS synth (~80–150 ms). A *local* LM removes the network leg; PersonaPlex full-duplex is ~160 ms by comparison — **the cascade trades ~1.5 s first-audio for smooth, controllable, any-model speech.**
274	
275	**Mapping to subaki-realtime:** the LM call becomes a server-side Next.js route (`app/api/llm/route.ts`) that streams the router's OpenAI-compatible response (SSE), keeping the HF token server-side like the existing `xai`/`openai` token-mint routes; a `engine: "cascade-hf" | "cascade-local"` entry in `lib/data.ts` plus a per-persona LM `model`/`provider`/`system_prompt` (parallel to `xai-agent.ts`) makes **local ↔ HF a one-field switch**. Full design in `~/Develop/voice-cascade/README.md`.
276	
277	## Tsubaki integration (assessed, not yet built)
278	
279	No WebRTC and no new web architecture needed — this is a direct-WebSocket engine like xAI (`lib/realtime/use-xai-session.ts`):
280	
281	- `use-moshi-session.ts` implementing `SessionApi`; provider entry `engine: "moshi"` → `ws://localhost:8998/api/chat`; per-persona `moshi-agent.ts` resolving voice/text prompts into query params.
282	- New piece: browser-side Opus (`opus-recorder` encode / `ogg-opus-decoder` decode) instead of PCM16-base64; playback reuses `PlaybackQueue` from `xai-audio.ts`.
283	- Full-duplex consequences: no user-side transcript (no ASR events), `interrupt()` is a no-op (model handles barge-in natively), `callState` derives from output audio activity.
284	- **Mic-gate the opening greeting** (see residual-glitch section): hold/threshold mic frames until the greeting completes, and set `autoGainControl:false` (keep `echoCancellation`/`noiseSuppression`), so ambient noise doesn't make the model interrupt its own greeting.
285

content.text:
I've reviewed the full branch and traced the cascade from mic to speaker. Here's the review, then the local-execution assessment anchored on [lib/data.ts](lib/data.ts).

## Part 1 — Review of `feat/cascade-voice-engine`

Five commits, +2672/−63. The shape is sound and consistent with the existing engine pattern (`use-xai-session`). What landed:

| Leg | Implementation | Where it runs |
|---|---|---|
| **STT** | Mistral realtime (`voxtral-mini-transcribe-realtime-2602`) over a Bun WS proxy that adds the `Bearer` header the browser can't → `api.mistral.ai`. Web Speech fallback. | **cloud** |
| **Turn detection** | Silero VAD, neural, `onnxruntime-web` WASM, jsDelivr-pinned. Hysteresis + redemption + manual Send. | **browser (local)** |
| **LM** | `/api/llm` → catalog-driven backend (`hf` router / `mistral`) → OpenAI-compatible SSE piped straight back. | **cloud** |
| **TTS** | `/api/mistral/tts` → `voxtral-mini-tts-2603` → per-clause MP3. `speechSynthesis` fallback. | **cloud** |

Things done well:
- **The LM leg is already backend-agnostic** — catalog (`config/lm-models.json`) + `resolveLmBackend`, route resolves URL+secret per request and pipes SSE verbatim. Adding a backend is a data edit.
- **Clause segmentation + promise-chained playback** ([use-cascade-session.ts:274](lib/realtime/use-cascade-session.ts#L274)) pipelines TTS against the LM stream — first audio doesn't wait for the full reply.
- **`autoGainControl:false`** carried over from the PersonaPlex mic-gate lesson so ambient noise doesn't trip the VAD. Good institutional memory.
- Failure handling is layered and non-fatal (VAD load fail → Send button; STT proxy down → Web Speech; TTS fail → `speechSynthesis`).

Two small asymmetries worth noting (not bugs):
- **TTS is *not* catalog-driven** the way the LM is — `app/api/mistral/tts/route.ts` hardcodes the Mistral URL + model. The LM got the config abstraction; TTS didn't.
- **`/api/llm` hard-requires a secret** ([route.ts:46-52](app/api/llm/route.ts#L46)) — `if (!apiKey) → 500`. That's correct for cloud backends but is the one thing blocking a keyless local backend.

## Part 2 — What "local" actually is today

`lib/data.ts` labels the MISTRAL row `exec: "local / remote"` — but **nothing model-related runs locally yet.** The only local pieces are Silero VAD and mic/audio capture. All three model legs (STT, LM, TTS) are cloud calls. The `docs/personaplex-local-inference.md` proves the local models work on your M5 Max (Voxtral STT 4.2 GB @ RTF 0.09, Voxtral TTS 4.0 GB @ RTF ≤0.42, ~8 GB combined; PersonaPlex q8 10.1 GB) and there's a working Python prototype at `~/Develop/voice-cascade/` with `engine="local"`/`"openai"` — but none of that is wired into the app.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The architecture already made a key decision for you: **"local" is a *backend* choice inside the cascade engine, not a new `Provider.engine`.** The engine (`cascade`) defines the STT→LM→TTS *topology*; each leg's endpoint is swappable. So local execution is mostly about extending the two remaining hardcoded legs to match the pattern the LM leg already has — plus one full-duplex exception (PersonaPlex) that genuinely *is* a different engine.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Part 3 — What's needed, leg by leg (easiest → hardest)

**① LM → local (nearly free).** A local OpenAI-compatible server (`llama-server`, `mlx-lm.server`, vLLM, LM Studio) is just a catalog entry pointing at `http://localhost:PORT/v1/chat/completions`. The route already speaks this protocol. **One code change:** make `envKey` optional so a keyless localhost backend doesn't 500. Add:
```jsonc
// config/lm-models.json → backends
"local": { "url": "http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions", "envKey": "", "supportsThinking": true }
```
and guard the route: skip the auth header when `envKey` is empty. That's the whole LM-local path.
